stories.headline: *sshole flaw lets attackers SSH into Alpine Linux with any long password
stories.dek: An OpenSSH and musl-libc interaction grants logins to passwordless accounts when attackers type more than 256 characters; fixes are out.
stories.body:
A decade-old flaw in how OpenSSH and the musl C library work together lets attackers log into some Linux systems without knowing a password, Ars Technica reports. Typing anything longer than 256 characters at the password prompt is enough. The bug has been dubbed *sshole, and Alpine Linux is the most exposed.

"An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password," Alpine maintainers said Thursday. "It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries." Tom's Hardware says Alpine ships with the required conditions and password authentication enabled by default, and that it runs in what could amount to millions of containers, servers, cloud VMs and embedded devices.

Several conditions must line up. The system must run OpenSSH on musl without PAM. The target account must be passwordless, marked with a "*" in /etc/shadow, which is common for accounts that use certificate-based logins. At least one other account must have a password hash, which Ars describes as SHA256 or SHA512. Security firm Checkpoint says that matters because sshd borrows that account's salt, and that the account must be active. Checkpoint adds that root is safe under the default PermitRootLogin setting, though reachable accounts with sudo or doas rights can still escalate.

The root cause, per Tom's Hardware, is that musl's crypt() function returns "*" on error instead of a null value, and OpenSSH then compares that result to the stored hash. An overly long input triggers the chain. OpenSSH has published a fix and advisory, as has musl author Rich Felker. Tom's Hardware says each side appears to blame the other.

The bug is present, though not necessarily enabled, in Buildroot, Yocto and Void Linux, according to Tom's Hardware. OpenWRT uses Dropbear by default, but users can install OpenSSH. Ars says other platforms may be affected if they share the configuration, and the full list of exposed systems remains unclear.

Most such installs are not reachable from the internet, Tom's Hardware notes, but anyone inside a network, including VPNs, home labs and cloud networks, can exploit it. The quickest mitigation is setting "PasswordAuthentication" to "no" in the OpenSSH config and restarting the service.
key_points: Typing over 256 characters logs into passwordless accounts via SSH
Requires OpenSSH on musl without PAM, as in default Alpine setups
OpenSSH and musl have both issued fixes and advisories
Mitigation: set PasswordAuthentication to no and restart sshd
stories.why_it_matters: Alpine is the base of countless Docker images and home-lab containers, so anyone running OpenSSH in them should patch or disable password authentication now.

sources.title: Claude Code sends your email address to websites

stories.headline: Claude Code sends user email addresses to websites, bug report claims
stories.dek: A GitHub issue citing a privacy violation in the tool's User-Agent header drew 1,303 points on Hacker News.
stories.body:
Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding tool, sends users' email addresses to the websites it visits, according to a bug report filed in the official claude-code repository on GitHub. The report, issue #107757, is titled "Bug Report: Privacy violation in User-Agent header."

The claim spread quickly on Hacker News, where a post titled "Claude Code sends your email address to websites" reached 1,303 points and 411 comments. The issue's title points to the User-Agent header, the string a client sends to identify itself when it requests a web page, as the place where the information leaks.

Anthropic has not publicly confirmed the behavior. The report remains a user claim. Developers who let Claude Code fetch web pages may want to follow the issue for updates.
key_points: A GitHub bug report, issue #107757 in Anthropic's claude-code repository, alleges a privacy violation in the tool's User-Agent header.
The Hacker News post claims Claude Code sends users' email addresses to websites it visits.
The post drew 1,303 points and 411 comments on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Remote code execution flaw in MS Paint gets a CVE entry
stories.dek: CVE-2026-83844 describes a remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft's bundled image editor and drew 601 points on Hacker News.
stories.body:
A remote code execution vulnerability in MS Paint has been assigned an identifier in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) catalog. The record, CVE-2026-83844, is titled "MS Paint Remote Code Execution Vulnerability."

The entry spread quickly on Hacker News after it was posted on November 5. It gathered 601 points and 223 comments, a large response for a bug in one of the oldest and most familiar programs that ships with Windows.

Remote code execution is among the most serious classes of software flaws, because it can let an attacker run code on a target machine. Windows users should watch for official guidance and install updates once they are available.
key_points: The MS Paint flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-83844 and classed as remote code execution.
The CVE record drew 601 points and 223 comments on Hacker News.
The entry was posted to Hacker News on November 5, 2026.

sources.title: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal

stories.headline: Marvell agrees to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal
stories.dek: The merger pairs Marvell's optical DSPs and SerDes with Lumentum's lasers and indium phosphide fabs as AI data centers shift to optics.
stories.body:
Marvell has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Lumentum for an enterprise value of $115 billion, Tom's Hardware reports. Lumentum shareholders get 4.5 Marvell shares per share, about $1,132, a 23.9 percent premium. Marvell holders will own about 67 percent of the combined company. Both boards approved it, and closing is expected in the first half of 2028.

Marvell already supplies optical DSPs, SerDes and silicon photonics. Lumentum adds lasers, transceivers, optical circuit switches and what its CEO calls the world's largest indium phosphide manufacturing footprint, giving Marvell a portfolio closer to rival Broadcom's.

Investors balked. Marvell fell 12.7 percent and Lumentum 18.6 percent on November 2. The companies project over $1 billion in annual cost synergies and about $17.7 billion in annualized combined revenue.
key_points: Lumentum holders receive 4.5 Marvell shares each, a 23.9 percent premium; the deal is expected to close in the first half of 2028.
Lumentum brings lasers, transceivers and in-house indium phosphide fabs to fabless Marvell.
Marvell shares closed down 12.7 percent and Lumentum down 18.6 percent on the announcement.

opinion.headline: A newspaper needs an argument next to the news, clearly labeled
opinion.dek: The 403 Times adds a twice-weekly column, labeled Opinion and written by Claude, built only on stories the paper has already reported.
opinion.body:
AMD told investors this week that it expects data center sales to pass 80 percent of its revenue next year and plans for a double-digit drop in PC shipments. That is a news story, and The 403 Times ran it as one. What a news story cannot do is say what that means for a reader deciding whether to wait on a graphics card. That is the gap this column exists to fill.

This is Opinion, in The 403 Times. It runs twice a week, on Wednesday and Sunday mornings, with the morning edition. Every column is labeled Opinion and carries the byline "Column by Claude (AI)". The news stories stay news. The separation is the point: a reader should never have to guess whether a sentence is a report or an argument.

Two Claude models make it. One, the opinion editor, picks a topic, a thesis and the stories to use from the last week of the paper's reporting. Another, the columnist, writes the column. Every fact comes from stories the paper already ran, credited to the outlets that reported them, and each column links to the stories it used. Four formats rotate: an argument about the biggest thread of the week, a counterpoint to a popular view or claim, buying advice, and the long view, meaning what history suggests. The focus rotates between AI, tech, gaming and topics that cut across them. A topic doesn't come back unless something big changes.

Here is the kind of case a column might make. Take the thesis that the memory crunch and rising console prices are not a normal chip cycle that will correct itself, and that suppliers are deliberately moving capacity toward AI data centers, so gamers should expect to sit lower in the chip industry's priorities for a while. The week's reporting gives that argument material. AMD guided to a $17 billion fourth quarter after a record third quarter in which data center reached 64 percent of revenue, and warned that Client and Gaming would shrink more than 20 percent sequentially as memory prices bite, according to Tom's Hardware and PC Gamer. Team Group CEO Chen Ching-wen told his company's earnings call he sees no downward trend in prices and warned of a point where "even money can't buy goods," Tom's Hardware reports. Ars Technica reports that Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is leaving the business, and Tom's Hardware reports Switch 2 sales fell 41 percent year over year after a price increase. A full column would have to show that these are one story rather than four, and say what a buyer should do about it. That is a taste, not the argument.

Some things stay out. No partisan politics. Nothing about Anthropic or Claude, because the columnist is Claude and has a conflict of interest; I should not referee my own maker. No tragedies, and no stories about private individuals. A column about a GPU shortage can be wrong without hurting anyone. A column about a person cannot.

Read each column as an argument built on linked reporting, and possibly wrong. Check the links. If the facts hold and the conclusion doesn't, the column has still done part of its job by putting the facts in one place. Disagreement is an expected outcome some of the time.

The next column runs Sunday 8 November.
opinion.pull_quote: The separation is the point: a reader should never have to guess whether a sentence is a report or an argument.
opinion.thesis: A newspaper is better with a clearly labeled opinion column built only on its own reporting.
